comparator.name: Criminologie
comparator.sourceNotes: The official 2026–2027 curriculum specifies a fixed 180-EC three-year bachelor: criminological and social-science foundations, legal study, two methods courses, three Research Lab stages, advanced criminology and criminal-law courses, a 15-EC minor, prevention and law-enforcement study, European justice, migration/diversity/crime, and a 15-EC analysis-and-reporting component. There are no formal bachelor routes requiring selection.
components: Open minor/exchange space in the third year.
European Law: Justice and Home Affairs

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Psychology, social behaviour and life-course development
Quantitative, qualitative and empirical criminological research
Crime prevention, public safety and policy evaluation
adjacent: Criminal justice, law, prevention and public safety
questions: Why does offending emerge and persist across people and social contexts?
How should law and public institutions prevent and respond to crime?

trace: provides an explicit framework for evaluating public interventions in terms of effectiveness, efficiency and distributional effects, supporting analysis of crime and safety policy
provides research design, sampling, survey and statistical foundations for empirical criminological research
provides practical data cleaning, visualisation and analysis skills for working with empirical social-science data
provides foundational legal, socio-legal and normative perspectives on law, including criminal law and justice
adds human-rights law and rights-based reasoning relevant to criminal-justice institutions and sanctions
directly studies criminal responsibility, guilt, defences, punishment, criminal case law and criminal justice
provides the international-law framework needed to understand cross-border legal cooperation and justice
examines constitutional and administrative limits on public authority, relevant to security governance and justice institutions
provides the EU-law framework within which European justice and cross-border cooperation operate
develops normative reasoning about responsibility, justice and punishment for evaluating criminal-justice choices
provides concepts of justice, authority and political obligation for analysing the legitimacy of criminal-justice institutions
provides comparative institutional analysis for understanding how political systems organise public safety and policy responses
examines international institutions, security and cross-border political cooperation relevant to transnational justice
examines EU institutions, power and policy-making relevant to European justice and security governance
analyses violence, radicalisation, conflict causation and prevention as adjacent public-safety phenomena without treating conflict as equivalent to ordinary criminality
introduces sociological concepts and theories for analysing the social causes and consequences of crime
provides qualitative research design, interviewing, interpretation and analysis skills relevant to criminological inquiry
develops sociological theory for explaining institutions, inequality and social change surrounding crime
adds advanced social theory on civil society, trust and solidarity relevant to social order and responses to crime
provides foundational psychological and behavioural science for evaluating individual-level explanations of offending
examines social influence, attitudes, groups and interpersonal behaviour relevant to offending, victimisation and social reactions
provides multivariate statistics and experimental methods for quantitative analysis of human behaviour
adds a biopsychosocial perspective on mental health and behaviour relevant to evaluating psychological explanations of offending; it is not used to equate mental disorder with criminality
develops advanced evidence synthesis, meta-analysis and R-based research skills for evaluating empirical claims
provides a life-course perspective on development that supports analysis of age-graded offending and criminal careers
examines youth radicalisation and evidence-based prevention, providing a concrete public-safety and prevention application
examines race, power, representation and marginalisation in media, supporting analysis of exclusion and social reactions around crime

alternatives.label: Crime, society & justice
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is a broad criminology-inspired programme combining sociology, psychology, criminal law, research methods, media, violence and international justice rather than a full specialist criminology sequence.
alternatives.concept: A closest feasible criminology programme combining social and psychological explanations of offending, criminal law and justice, quantitative and qualitative research, victimisation, exclusion, prevention and cross-border justice.
progression: Legal, sociological, political and behavioural foundations precede advanced criminal-law, social-theory, psychology and research work; the sociology sequence progresses from Introduction through Modern Sociology to advanced contemporary theory, and all formal prerequisites and term offerings are satisfied.

alternatives.label: Criminal justice, law & public safety
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is visibly organised around criminal justice, public authority, EU governance, policy evaluation and normative questions of punishment while retaining criminology-relevant social science and methods.
alternatives.concept: A criminal-justice and public-safety route centred on law, punishment, public institutions, prevention, policy evaluation and European justice, supported by sociology, psychology and empirical methods.
alternatives.distinctness: Political philosophy, EU politics, public economics and ethics replace advanced clinical/developmental psychology and prevention-research courses, shifting the organising logic from broad criminological explanation toward institutions, law and public policy.
progression: Law and social-science foundations precede advanced criminal justice, EU politics, public economics and social theory; Research Methods & Statistics precedes Public Economics, and all formal prerequisites and term offerings are satisfied.

candidates.label: Criminal justice, law, prevention and public safety

selection.assessment: The evidence supports one genuinely different additional route around criminal justice, law, prevention and public safety. All other generator-eligible interests are integral to the broad criminology core, and the remaining support/search-only rows do not justify a third independent organising concept.

blocks: European Law: Justice and Home Affairs is narrower than UCR Foundations of European Union Law, but both substantially concern the EU legal order; the match is limited to the shared EU-law foundation.
Both are advanced research-training components; UCR Advanced Research Seminar emphasises evidence synthesis, meta-analysis and R rather than a criminology-specific research lab.

notes.text: The Erasmus bachelor provides a dedicated criminology sequence with specialised criminological theory, crime measurement, criminal careers, formal and material criminal law, law-enforcement study and a three-stage criminology research-lab sequence. UCR can build strong crime-and-justice programmes, but it does not reproduce that full disciplinary and professional sequence.
